name: Quakers
info: The Quakers, or Religious Society of Friends, are a Christian movement that arose in mid-17th-century England and spread overseas, stressing the inward light, worship without clergy, and testimonies against oaths, war and slavery.

facts.where: England and Wales, Ireland, the Netherlands, Barbados and the American colonies from the 17th century; today chiefly Africa (49% of adult Friends in 2017) and North America (22%), with Kenya, the United States, Burundi and Bolivia holding the most
facts.period: arose in mid-17th-century England; persecuted until the Act of Toleration 1689; Quietist period in the 18th century; splits in the 19th century; Quaker Renaissance from the late 19th century; worldwide and still active
facts.figures: George Fox, the founder; Margaret Fell, who with Fox developed new conceptions of family and community; Robert Barclay, divine; William Penn, founder of Pennsylvania; Mary Dyer, hanged in Boston in 1660; Elias Hicks, Joseph John Gurney and John Wilbur, around whom nineteenth-century branches formed; Rufus Jones and John Wilhelm Rowntree of the Quaker Renaissance
facts.outcome: persecution in England ended after 1689; the numbers fell in the 18th and 19th centuries and the Society divided into branches; Friends became known for opposition to slavery and war, for business and schools, and for relief work, sharing the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947

sections.background:
Religious strife in the Kingdom of England had lasted for centuries, with proto-Protestant groups, mainly the Lollards, appearing before the English Reformation brought radical ideas into the mainstream. During and after the English Civil War (1642–1651) many dissenting Christian groups emerged, among them the Seekers. George Fox, a young man, was dissatisfied with the teachings of the Church of England and of the nonconformists.

While living in Mansfield, Nottinghamshire, in 1647, Fox claimed to have received a revelation that "there is one, even Christ Jesus, who can speak to thy condition", and became convinced that a direct experience of Christ was possible without the aid of ordained clergy. In 1652 he had a vision on Pendle Hill in Lancashire, in which he believed that "the Lord let me see in what places he had a great people to be gathered". He then travelled around England, the Netherlands and Barbados preaching, and he considered himself to be restoring a true, "pure" Christian church.

The name Quaker began in 1650, when Fox was brought before the magistrates Gervase Bennet and Nathaniel Barton on a charge of blasphemy. According to Fox's autobiography, Bennet was the first to call them Quakers, because Fox bade them tremble at the word of the Lord. The members also used names such as Friends of Truth, Children of the Light and Saints for themselves.
sections.aims:
Friends are generally united by a belief in each human's ability to be guided by the inward light, and they have traditionally professed a priesthood of all believers. Their central message was that "Christ has come to teach his people himself". Isaac Penington wrote in 1670 that "it is not enough to hear of Christ, or read of Christ, but this is the thing, to feel him to be my root, my life, and my foundation". To differing extents Friends avoid creeds and hierarchical structures, and their doctrines have only at times been set down in statements of faith, such as Robert Barclay's An Apology for the True Christian Divinity (1678) and the Richmond Declaration of Faith (1887).

Early Friends focused their private lives on behaviour and speech reflecting the light of God, with the goal of Christian perfection. They wore plain dress, practised teetotalism, refused to swear oaths or take part in war, and opposed slavery. Many refused the usual names of the days of the week and of the months, which came from pagan deities, and used a plain calendar of First Day to Seventh Day and First Month to Twelfth Month.

Worship in the tradition of Fox is unprogrammed: Friends gather in expectant waiting upon God, and anyone who feels led to speak may do so. Church business is conducted in the same manner, with no voting; a decision is reached when the meeting as a whole feels that the way forward has been discerned.
sections.events:
Quakerism gained a considerable following in England and Wales, not least among women, and the number of Quakers rose to a peak of 60,000 by 1680. The dominant Protestant discourse regarded them as a blasphemous challenge to social and political order, and they were persecuted under the Quaker Act 1662 and the Conventicle Act 1664. The persecution eased after the Declaration of Indulgence (1687–1688) and stopped under the Act of Toleration 1689.

In North America persecution began in July 1656, when Mary Fisher and Ann Austin began preaching in Boston; they were imprisoned in harsh conditions for five weeks and banished by the Massachusetts Bay Colony, and their books were burned. In 1660 Mary Dyer was hanged near Boston Common, one of four executed Quakers known as the Boston martyrs. In 1661 Charles II forbade Massachusetts from executing anyone for professing Quakerism. West Jersey and Pennsylvania were established by William Penn in 1676 and 1682, and he signed a peace treaty with Tamanend, leader of the Lenape; the peace endured almost a century, until the Penn's Creek Massacre of 1755.

In the 18th century Friends became more inward-looking and less active in converting others, and numbers in England and Wales fell to 19,800 by 1800 and 13,859 by 1860. Around the American Revolutionary War some Friends split off over support for the war, forming the Free Quakers and the Universal Friends. Elias Hicks's preaching precipitated the Great Separation of 1827, and in 1842 John Wilbur was expelled from his yearly meeting.
sections.people:
George Fox was the movement's founder. With Margaret Fell, the wife of the judge Thomas Fell, he developed new conceptions of family and community that stressed "holy conversation", and the two saw the Quaker mother as essential to it. Early ministers who travelled preaching were known as the Valiant Sixty, and some of them were women. Mary Fisher and Ann Austin preached in Boston, Mary Dyer was hanged there, and Quaker women published at least 220 texts in the 17th century. Robert Barclay was a Quaker divine, and William Penn, an affluent Quaker, founded West Jersey and Pennsylvania.

In the 19th century Elias Hicks, Joseph John Gurney and John Wilbur gave their names to branches: the Hicksites, who tended to be agrarian and poorer, the Gurneyites, who grew more evangelical, and the Conservative Friends, or Wilburites. Isaac Crewdson's book A Beacon to the Society of Friends (1835) led to his resignation, with 48 fellow members of Manchester Meeting and about 250 other British Quakers in 1836–1837. Rufus Jones, John Wilhelm Rowntree and Edward Grubb stood behind the liberal Quaker Renaissance.

Opposition to slavery came from Benjamin Lay, Anthony Benezet and John Woolman, and later from Levi Coffin and Isaac Hopper, who helped enslaved people escape through the Underground Railroad. The black Quaker Paul Cuffe, a sea captain and businessman, was active in the abolitionist and resettlement movement, and Laura Smith Haviland established the first station of the Underground Railroad in Michigan.
sections.outcomes:
Official persecution in England ended in 1689, but the Society later declined and divided. Numbers fell to 13,859 in England and Wales by 1860. The Hicksite–Orthodox split arose from ideological and socioeconomic tensions: Orthodox Quakers, with growing financial success, wanted to "transform their sect into a church", while Hicksites generally saw the market economy as corrupting. British Quakers recognised only the Orthodox and refused to correspond with the Hicksites. The Fritchley General Meeting, formed in 1865 by Friends who left London Yearly Meeting, stayed separate until 1968.

On slavery, owning enslaved people had been fairly common among Friends in colonial America, for example in Pennsylvania, but by the American Revolutionary War few Friends owned slaves. Nine of the twelve founding members of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade were Quakers. Because Quakers could not serve as Members of Parliament, they relied on Anglican men such as William Wilberforce. In the 1830s the abolitionist Grimké sisters dissociated themselves from the Quakers when they saw that Black Quakers were segregated in separate pews in the Philadelphia meeting house.

Exemption from military service was first granted to Quakers in Great Britain in 1757, a milestone in freedom of conscience. In both world wars many Friends became conscientious objectors, and the British Friends Service Council and the American Friends Service Committee shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947.
sections.legacy:
In 2017 there were an estimated 377,557 adult Quakers, 49% of them in Africa and 22% in North America. Kenya had 119,200, the United States 80,000, Burundi 47,600 and Bolivia 28,500. About 11% of Quakers worldwide practise unprogrammed worship, the dominant form in Britain, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and parts of the United States; some 40% belong to the evangelical branch, with a pastor and a prepared Bible message. The Britain Yearly Meeting had 14,260 adult members, a number that has declined steadily since the mid-20th century.

Views within the Society range from evangelical, holiness and conservative to liberal Christianity, to Universalist Friends, who affirm religious pluralism, and to a minority of non-theists. Non-theism is controversial, and some Christian Quakers in Britain Yearly Meeting have called for non-theists to be denied membership. The Friends World Committee for Consultation loosely unifies the different traditions.

Quakers founded banks including Barclays and Lloyds, firms such as Cadbury, Rowntree, Fry and Clarks, and schools. Abraham Darby I and Edward Pease were prominent in ironmaking and the Stockton and Darlington Railway. Eric Baker was a founder of Amnesty International and of the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament, Edith Pye established the Famine Relief Committee that led to Oxfam, and Irving and Dorothy Stowe co-founded Greenpeace in 1971. In 2007 David Yount, author of How the Quakers Invented America, argued that Quakers first introduced ideas such as trial by jury, equal rights for men and women, and public education.

summary: The Quakers, or Religious Society of Friends, arose in mid-17th-century England around George Fox, who taught that Christ could teach his people directly. Persecuted in England and Massachusetts, they became known for opposing slavery and war, and numbered an estimated 377,557 adults in 2017, most of them in Africa.
references: Margaret Hope Bacon, The Quiet Rebels: The Story of the Quakers in America (Pendle Hill Publications, 2000)
Hugh Barbour, The Quakers in Puritan England (Friends United Press, 1985)
